newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israeli El Al denies doomed plane bore missiles.
newsitem.headline: Israeli El Al denies doomed plane bore missiles.

text.p: Israel's El Al airlines denied a newspaper report on Tuesday that a cargo plane which crashed into an Amsterdam suburb in 1992, killing at least 42 people, carried missiles.
The report by Israel's Yedioth Ahronoth newspaper also said that hundreds of kilograms of depleted uranium used as ballast in the Boeing 747 was missing following the crash.
Spokesman Nachman Klieman, reacting to the report, said the El Al plane carried military spare parts. But he denied any missiles or explosive materials were aboard.
The newspaper said a cargo manifest had shown a list of 189 military items, including not only spare military parts and various electronic items but also Sidewinder air-to-air missiles.

"There's absolutely nothing new in the story," Klieman said. "As I said four years ago there were military parts for replacement -- nothing in any way, shape or form resembling a missile. There were replacement parts for fighter planes and other military equipment."
He said cargo could be off-loaded at the last minute because of weight concerns -- and the manifest changed.
"What counts is the final cargo manifest and that is what the Dutch authorities took from El Al the evening of the accident," Klieman said.
He said civilian aircraft manufacturers all over the world, including Boeing, used depleted uranium for ballast in the tail section of airplanes. He said a small amount provided sufficient weight.
Depleted uranium was not only safe but also permitted by federal aviation authorities in the United States and Europe, he said.
Yedioth Ahronoth said its investigation showed only 160 kilograms of the uranium had been found immediately after the crash but from 400 to 600 kilograms were used in the plane.
"Nobody knows exactly how much is in there because every aircraft is different," Klieman countered.
"To the best of our knowledge and understanding no government authorities throughout the world would allow the use of materials of this type for ballast if it presented a safety problem," he said.
